stops.note: from mantra 'counsel'; the Arthashastra, the ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, advises the king to rule with a council of mantrins
Sanskrit statecraft terms entered Malay through Indianised courts such as Srivijaya; the Malacca Sultanate used menteri for its royal ministers
picked up after Afonso de Albuquerque took Malacca in 1511, and reshaped to echo Portuguese mandar 'to command'; from Macau (settled 1557) they applied it to Ming Chinese officials
first appears in Robert Parke's 1588 English translation of Juan González de Mendoza's history of China; the officials' spoken language and, from the 1770s, the small orange later took the name too

current_meaning: the standard spoken form of Chinese; a powerful bureaucrat; a small loose-skinned orange
